This mock exam covers all six lectures of the course. It has 100
points. Your final grade is the number of points divided by 10, rounded to a
whole or half grade. You pass with 55 points or more.

You take the Intermediate exam in TestVision. It lasts 120 minutes. You may
use RStudio, Excel, the calculator in TestVision, a simple pocket
calculator, and scrap paper. The practice
exam in TestVision appears in your own TestVision account once the
lecturer publishes it. You log in with your university account. There is no separate
link. General information about TestVision for students is on the
[university page about TestVision](https://www.tilburguniversity.edu/students/studying/exams/e-assessment/testvision).

You receive the [QM Intermediate Code Sheet](code-sheet.qmd) at
the exam. Keep it open while you work on this mock exam.

Use 120 minutes as the practice time limit, as in the exam.

## How this mock exam works

This mock exam gives an impression of what an exam in this course can look
like. You download a data file, you run R yourself, and you type your answers.

All parts are open questions. You type a number with your calculation, or
one to three sentences. An answer without a calculation or an explanation
gets no points, unless the part asks only to report or to state something.

A part that starts with "In R:" needs code that you write and run yourself.
Paste the R code that you used into your answer, and type the numbers that
the part asks for. If a part asks you to make a plot, describe
what you see in words. You do not need to paste the plot, but paste the
code that made it. You can answer all other parts from your own results, from printed
output, or with a short calculation. You may use R as a calculator
everywhere.

Most parts give a structure for your answer. Copy it into the answer field
and fill in each line.

Report all numerical results with at least three significant digits.

All tests in this course are two-sided. Use a 5% significance level.

## Dataset used throughout

Treat the practice data as a simple random sample of 320
young ventures from a business registry. One row is one venture. The data
are observational: none of the predictors was assigned by chance.

- `growth_pct`: growth of annual sales compared with the year before, in
  percent. A value of 12 means that sales were 12% higher than in the year
  before.
- `marketing_10k`: annual marketing spending, in €10,000s. The values run
  from 0.25 (€2,500) to 7.99 (€79,900).
- `experience_years`: prior industry experience of the lead founder, in
  years, from 0 to 18.
- `team_size`: number of current team members, from 1 to 10.
- `digital`: `No` for a mainly physical offering and `Yes` for a mainly
  digital offering. `No` is the reference category.
- `spend_c`: `marketing_10k - 4`, marketing spending centred at €40,000.
  This is close to the sample mean of about €40,400.

The population is the set of ventures in this registry. The practice data
are invented. The code that made them is in a collapsed box at the end of
this page. It is not part of the exam.

[Download `qm-intermediate-mock-exam.csv`](../data/qm-intermediate-mock-exam.csv),
save it in the folder `data` of your R project, and load it with the code
below. If you save the file directly in your project folder, write
`"qm-intermediate-mock-exam.csv"` as the file name.

```{r}
#| label: imock-load
ventures <- read.csv("data/qm-intermediate-mock-exam.csv")
ventures$digital <- factor(ventures$digital, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
```

## Question 1: Simple regression (15 points)

A founder asks whether ventures that spend more on marketing grow faster.
The outcome is `growth_pct` and the predictor is `marketing_10k`.

1. In R: load the data. Write down your R code, the number of rows, the
   mean of `growth_pct`, and the largest value of `growth_pct`. Use (copy
   and paste) this structure: **(2 points)**

   ```text
   R code:
   Number of rows:
   Mean of growth_pct:
   Largest value of growth_pct:
   ```

2. In R: fit the simple regression of `growth_pct` on `marketing_10k`.
   Write down your R code, the intercept, the slope, and an interpretation
   of the slope in one sentence. Use (copy and paste) this structure:
   **(7 points)**

   ```text
   R code:
   Intercept:
   Slope:
   Interpretation of the slope:
   ```

3. In R: a venture spends €50,000 on marketing, and its actual sales
   growth is 11%. Use the model of part 2 to calculate the fitted growth of
   this venture. Write down your R code, the fitted growth, the residual with
   its calculation, and one sentence on what the sign of the residual means
   for this venture. Use (copy and paste) this structure: **(6 points)**

   ```text
   R code:
   Fitted growth:
   Residual:
   Meaning of the sign:
   ```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Model answer

**Code**

```{r}
#| label: imock-q1-fit
# Part 1
ventures <- read.csv("data/qm-intermediate-mock-exam.csv")
ventures$digital <- factor(ventures$digital, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
nrow(ventures)
mean(ventures$growth_pct)
max(ventures$growth_pct)

# Part 2
simple_model <- lm(growth_pct ~ marketing_10k, data = ventures)
coef(simple_model)

# Part 3
fit_50k <- predict(simple_model, newdata = data.frame(marketing_10k = 5))
fit_50k
11 - fit_50k
```

**Answers**

1. Filled-in structure:
   - R code: see the code above, part 1.
   - Number of rows: 320
   - Mean of growth_pct: 12.172
   - Largest value of growth_pct: 31.94
2. Filled-in structure:
   - R code: see the code above, part 2.
   - Intercept: 6.598
   - Slope: 1.378
   - Interpretation of the slope: among the 320 sampled ventures, a venture
     that spends €10,000 more on marketing is associated with sales growth
     that is on average 1.38 percentage points higher.
3. Filled-in structure:
   - R code: see the code above, part 3. €50,000 is `marketing_10k = 5`.
   - Fitted growth: 13.49%
   - Residual: $11-13.49=-2.49$ percentage points
   - Meaning of the sign: the residual is negative, so this venture grew
     less than the fitted growth for ventures with the same marketing
     spending.
:::

Check the model of Question 1, `growth_pct ~ marketing_10k`. Parts 1 and 3

1. In R: make the residual-versus-fitted plot of the model. Write down

   pattern in the plot that shows this, in one or two sentences per

   ```text
   Linearity:
   Homoskedasticity:
   ```

2. Some ventures in this model have a large standardised residual or a
   large Cook's distance. A colleague wants to delete all of them, "to get a
   cleaner model". Write down the rule for flagged observations in one
   sentence. Then describe in one or two sentences what you would do with
   these ventures. Use (copy and paste) this structure: **(4 points)**

   ```text
   Rule for flagged observations:
   What I would do with these ventures:
   ```

3. In R: make the normal Q-Q plot of the standardised residuals. Write
   down your R code and describe in one sentence how the points lie relative
   to the line. Then explain in one sentence whether a departure from
   normality is a serious problem for this model with 320 ventures, and
   why. Use (copy and paste) this structure: **(6 points)**

   ```text
   R code:
   How the points lie relative to the line:
   Serious problem for this model? Why:
   ```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Model answer

**Code**

```{r}
#| label: imock-q2-resid-plot
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Model answer, part 1: residuals against fitted values of the simple model of sales growth on marketing spending."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of residuals against fitted sales growth from about 7 to 18 percent. The points scatter around the dashed zero line without a clear curve. Their vertical spread is narrower on the left and wider on the right, like a funnel."
# Part 1
plot(fitted(simple_model), residuals(simple_model),
     xlab = "Fitted value", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: imock-q2-qq-plot
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Model answer, part 3: normal Q-Q plot of the standardised residuals of the simple model."
#| fig-alt: "Normal Q-Q plot. The points lie close to the straight reference line over most of the range and bend slightly above it at the right end, with the largest standardised residual at about 3.4."
# Part 3
qqnorm(rstandard(simple_model))
qqline(rstandard(simple_model))
```

**Answers**

1. Filled-in structure:
   - R code: see the code above, part 1.
   - Linearity: the residuals lie around zero along the whole range of
     fitted values, with at most a slight bend at the ends. Linearity is
     roughly met. A straight line is a reasonable first summary. Question 5
     checks whether a curve fits better.
   - Homoskedasticity: the vertical spread of the residuals grows from left
     to right, with the fitted growth. The points spread out like a funnel. This is
     heteroskedasticity, so homoskedasticity (constant variance of the
     errors) is likely not met. The spread of the residuals is about 1.6
     times larger at the right end than at the left end.
2. Filled-in structure:
   - Rule for flagged observations: investigate, report, never silently
     delete.
   - What I would do with these ventures: look at the flagged ventures in
     the data and ask whether a value is an error or whether the venture is
     of a different kind. Then fit the model with and without these
     ventures, show both results, and say which one I use and why.
3. Filled-in structure:
   - R code: see the code above, part 3.
   - How the points lie relative to the line: they follow the line in the
     middle. At the upper end they lie above the line, and near the lower
     end slightly below it.
   - Serious problem for this model? Why: no. Normal errors matter in small
     samples. With 320 ventures the tests and intervals still hold
     approximately.
:::

```{r}
#| label: imock-q2-spread-check
#| include: false
# Checks the funnel of part 1: spread of the residuals by third of fitted growth.
thirds <- cut(
  fitted(simple_model),
  breaks = quantile(fitted(simple_model), c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1)),
  include.lowest = TRUE, labels = c("lowest", "middle", "highest")
)
tapply(residuals(simple_model), thirds, sd)
```

## Question 3: Inference and fit (14 points)

A colleague drew 200 of the 320 ventures at random and fitted the model
below to these 200 ventures. You do not know which ventures she drew, so you
cannot run this model yourself. Answer from her output. The formulas are on
the code sheet.

```text
Call:
lm(formula = growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + experience_years + 
    digital, data = ventures_200)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-11.2970  -2.7338  -0.0992   2.6132  12.3786 

Coefficients:
                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)       2.73159    0.78897   3.462 0.000658 ***
marketing_10k     1.35473    0.12868  10.528  < 2e-16 ***
experience_years  0.28585    0.05277   5.417 1.77e-07 ***
digitalYes        3.17544    0.58246   5.452 1.49e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.049 on 196 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4803,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.4723 
F-statistic: 60.38 on 3 and 196 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
```

For this model, SSE = 3212.85 and SST = 6181.93. The critical value for a
95% confidence interval and a 5% test with 196 degrees of freedom is
$t_{0.975,\,196}=1.972$.

1. Write down the calculation of the Multiple R-squared from SSE and SST,
   with the formula and the values you use. Then state in one sentence what
   this number says about the model for these 200 ventures. Use (copy and
   paste) this structure: **(5 points)**

   ```text
   Calculation of R-squared:
   What it says about the model:
   ```

2. Calculate the 95% confidence interval for the coefficient of
   `marketing_10k`. Write down the formula, the values you use, the margin
   of error, and the lower and upper bound, showing your calculations. Then
   state whether the two-sided test at the 5% level rejects a coefficient
   of zero, and explain in one or two sentences how the interval shows
   this. Use (copy and paste) this structure: **(9 points)**

   ```text
   Formula:
   Values used:
   Margin of error:
   Lower bound:
   Upper bound:
   Conclusion of the test, and how the interval shows it:
   ```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Model answer

**Answers**

1. Filled-in structure:
   - Calculation of R-squared:

     $$
     R^2=1-\text{SSE}/\text{SST}=1-3212.85/6181.93=0.480
     $$

   - What it says about the model: among these 200 ventures, the model
     explains 48.0% of the variation in sales growth.
2. Filled-in structure:
   - Formula: $\hat\beta_j\pm t_{0.975,\,df}\,\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)$,
     with

     $$
     df=n-k-1=200-3-1=196
     $$

   - Values used: $\hat\beta_j=1.35473$,
     $\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)=0.12868$, $t_{0.975,\,196}=1.972$
   - Margin of error: $1.972\times0.12868=0.254$
   - Lower bound: $1.355-0.254=1.10$ percentage points per €10,000
   - Upper bound: $1.355+0.254=1.61$ percentage points per €10,000
   - Conclusion of the test, and how the interval shows it: zero lies
     outside the interval. The interval contains the values of the
     coefficient that the two-sided 5% test does not reject, so the test
     rejects a coefficient of zero. At the 5% level we can conclude the
     following for all ventures in the registry: at the same experience and
     offering type, more marketing spending goes with higher sales growth.
:::

```{r}
#| label: imock-colleague
#| include: false
# Checks the printed output of the colleague in Question 3.
set.seed(2026)
rows_200 <- sort(sample(nrow(ventures), 200))
ventures_200 <- ventures[rows_200, ]
model_200 <- lm(
  growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + experience_years + digital,
  data = ventures_200
)
summary(model_200)
SSE_200 <- sum(residuals(model_200)^2)
SST_200 <- sum((ventures_200$growth_pct - mean(ventures_200$growth_pct))^2)
c(SSE = SSE_200, SST = SST_200, R2 = 1 - SSE_200 / SST_200)
qt(0.975, df.residual(model_200))
confint(model_200)["marketing_10k", ]
```

## Question 4: Multiple regression and a dummy predictor (23 points)

The table below has the layout of a regression table in a research paper.
It shows three models of sales growth (`growth_pct`), fitted to all 320
ventures of the practice data. You do not need to run these models for
parts 1 and 2.

::: {.reg-table}
| | (1) | (2) | (3) |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| Marketing spending (€10,000s) | 1.340\*\*\* | 1.338\*\*\* | 1.341\*\*\* |
| | (0.106) | (0.100) | (0.100) |
| Digital offering (1 = yes) | 2.969\*\*\* | 3.016\*\*\* | 3.084\*\*\* |
| | (0.488) | (0.462) | (0.463) |
| Founder experience (years) | | 0.255\*\*\* | 0.258\*\*\* |
| | | (0.042) | (0.041) |
| Team size (members) | | | 0.168 |
| | | | (0.103) |
| Intercept | 5.418\*\*\* | 3.206\*\*\* | 2.449\*\* |
| | (0.528) | (0.617) | (0.771) |
| Observations | 320 | 320 | 320 |
| $R^2$ | 0.395 | 0.459 | 0.464 |
| Adjusted $R^2$ | 0.391 | 0.454 | 0.457 |
:::

Outcome: sales growth (%). Ordinary least squares. Standard errors in
parentheses. All three columns use the same 320 ventures. The reference
category of the dummy is ventures with a mainly physical offering.
\* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001.

The critical value for a 95% confidence interval and a 5% test is
$t_{0.975,\,df}=1.967$ in all three columns.

1. Test in five steps whether team size is individually significant in
   column (3), with the critical value approach at the 5% level. Write
   down the null and the alternative hypothesis, the formula of the test
   statistic, the rejection rule, the value of the test statistic with its
   calculation, and your conclusion in words. Then state in one sentence
   what the missing star of team size means. Use (copy and paste) this
   structure: **(6 points)**

   ```text
   Null hypothesis H0:          and alternative hypothesis H1:
   Test statistic formula:
   Rejection rule:
   Value of the test statistic:
   Conclusion:
   Meaning of the missing star:
   ```

2. Venture B spends €30,000 more on marketing than venture A. Its lead
   founder has 4 more years of experience. B has a digital offering and A a
   physical one. Both have the same team size. Calculate the fitted growth
   of B minus the fitted growth of A with column (3). Write down the
   contribution of each predictor with its calculation, and the resulting
   difference with its unit. Use (copy and paste) this structure:
   **(6 points)**

   ```text
   Calculation:
   Fitted growth of B minus fitted growth of A:
   ```

3. In R: test whether founder experience and team size are jointly useful
   in the model of column (3), compared with the model of column (1), with
   the p-value approach at the 5% level. Write down your R code, the null
   and the alternative hypothesis, the formula of the test statistic, the
   values you fill into the formula, the value of the test statistic with
   its calculation, the p-value, and your conclusion in words. Then explain
   in one sentence how your conclusion and the missing star of team size
   can both be true. Use (copy and paste) this structure: **(11 points)**

   ```text
   R code:
   Null hypothesis H0:          and alternative hypothesis H1:
   Test statistic formula:
   Values in the formula:
   Value of the test statistic:
   P-value:
   Conclusion:
   Why the conclusion and the missing star can both be true:
   ```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Model answer

**Code**

```{r}
#| label: imock-q4-anova
# Part 3
col_1 <- lm(growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + digital, data = ventures)
col_3 <- lm(
  growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + digital + experience_years + team_size,
  data = ventures
)
anova(col_1, col_3)
```

**Answers**

1. Filled-in structure:
   - Null hypothesis H0 and alternative hypothesis H1:
     $H_0:\beta_{team}=0$ and $H_1:\beta_{team}\ne0$, where $\beta_{team}$
     is the coefficient of team size in the model of column (3) for all
     ventures of the registry.
   - Test statistic formula:
     $T=\hat\beta_{team}/\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_{team})$, which has the
     $t_{315}$ distribution if $H_0$ is true.
   - Rejection rule: reject $H_0$ if $|t_{obs}|\ge t_{0.975,\,315}=1.967$.
   - Value of the test statistic: the numbers in parentheses are standard
     errors, so

     $$
     t_{obs}=0.168/0.103=1.63.
     $$

   - Conclusion: $|1.63|<1.967$, so do not reject $H_0$. At the 5% level we
     cannot conclude that team size goes with growth at fixed marketing
     spending, offering type, and experience.
   - Meaning of the missing star: the p-value of team size is above 0.05,
     so its coefficient is not significantly different from zero at the 5%
     level.
2. Filled-in structure:
   - Calculation: marketing, €30,000 is 3 steps of €10,000, so
     $3\times1.341=4.023$. Experience: $4\times0.258=1.032$. Digital
     offering: 3.084.
   - Fitted growth of B minus fitted growth of A:
     $4.023+1.032+3.084=8.14$ percentage points
3. Filled-in structure:
   - R code: see the code above, part 3.
   - Null hypothesis H0 and alternative hypothesis H1: $H_0$: the
     coefficients of founder experience and team size are both zero. $H_1$:
     at least one of them is not zero.
   - Test statistic formula:
     $F=\dfrac{(\text{SSE}_R-\text{SSE}_C)/q}{\text{SSE}_C/(n-k_C-1)}$
   - Values in the formula: $\text{SSE}_R=5949.3$ (column 1),
     $\text{SSE}_C=5272.6$ (column 3), $q=2$, $n-k_C-1=315$
   - Value of the test statistic:

     $$
     F=\dfrac{(5949.3-5272.6)/2}{5272.6/315}=\dfrac{338.35}{16.74}=20.2
     $$

   - P-value: 5.491e-09, that is 0.00000000549
   - Conclusion: the p-value is far below 0.05, so reject $H_0$. At the 5%
     level we can conclude that the two predictors together improve the
     model of column (1).
   - Why the conclusion and the missing star can both be true: the F-test
     asks about the two terms together, and the t-test asks about team size
     alone. The joint result comes from experience. A set of terms can be
     jointly significant while one of its terms is not significant.
:::

```{r}
#| label: imock-q4-table
#| include: false
# Checks the regression table and the answers to parts 1 to 3 of Question 4.
col_2 <- lm(growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + digital + experience_years,
            data = ventures)
summary(col_1)
summary(col_2)
summary(col_3)
qt(0.975, df.residual(col_3))
b3 <- coef(col_3)
unname(3 * b3["marketing_10k"] + 4 * b3["experience_years"] + b3["digitalYes"])
confint(col_3)
cor(ventures$marketing_10k, ventures$experience_years)
((deviance(col_1) - deviance(col_3)) / 2) /
  (deviance(col_3) / df.residual(col_3))
```

## Question 5: Interactions and curvature (20 points)

Part 1 asks whether marketing spending goes with more growth for digital
ventures than for physical ventures. Parts 2 and 3 use a model in which the
relation between marketing spending and growth can be curved.

1. In R: fit a model of sales growth (`growth_pct`) with marketing
   spending centred at €40,000 (`spend_c`), the offering type (`digital`),
   the interaction of the two, and founder experience
   (`experience_years`). Write down your R code and the coefficients of
   `spend_c`, `digitalYes`, and the interaction. Then write down the
   marketing slope for physical ventures, the marketing slope for digital
   ventures with its calculation, and an interpretation of the interaction
   coefficient in one sentence. Use (copy and paste) this structure:
   **(10 points)**

   ```text
   R code:
   Coefficient of spend_c:
   Coefficient of digitalYes:
   Coefficient of the interaction:
   Marketing slope for physical ventures:
   Marketing slope for digital ventures:
   Interpretation of the interaction coefficient:
   ```

2. In R: fit a model of sales growth (`growth_pct`) with marketing spending
   (`marketing_10k`), the square of marketing spending, the offering type
   (`digital`), and founder experience (`experience_years`), without an
   interaction. Write down your R code and the coefficients of marketing
   spending and of its square. Then write down, with the formula and your
   calculation, the fitted change in growth when marketing spending rises
   from €20,000 to €30,000, and when it rises from €60,000 to €70,000.
   Offering type and experience stay fixed. State in one sentence what the
   two results show together. Use (copy and paste) this structure:
   **(7 points)**

   ```text
   R code:
   Coefficient of marketing spending:
   Coefficient of its square:

   ```

3. A founder plans to spend €150,000 on marketing. She wants to use the

   ```text
   First reason:
   Second reason:
   ```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Model answer

**Code**

```{r}
#| label: imock-q5-interaction
# Part 1
interaction_model <- lm(
  growth_pct ~ spend_c * digital + experience_years,
  data = ventures
)
coef(interaction_model)
```

```{r}
#| label: imock-q5-quadratic
# Part 2
curve_model <- lm(
  growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + I(marketing_10k^2) + digital +
    experience_years,
  data = ventures
)
coef(curve_model)
```

**Answers**

1. Filled-in structure:
   - R code: see the code above, part 1.
   - Coefficient of spend_c: 1.044
   - Coefficient of digitalYes: 2.967
   - Coefficient of the interaction: 0.660 (`spend_c:digitalYes`)
   - Marketing slope for physical ventures: 1.044 percentage points per
     €10,000
   - Marketing slope for digital ventures: $1.044+0.660=1.704$ percentage
     points per €10,000
   - Interpretation of the interaction coefficient: among the 320 sampled
     ventures and at the same founder experience, each additional €10,000 of
     marketing spending goes with 0.660 percentage points more sales growth
     for digital ventures than for physical ventures.
2. Filled-in structure:
   - R code: see the code above, part 2.
   - Coefficient of marketing spending: 2.179
   - Coefficient of its square: $-0.105$
   - Fitted change from €20,000 to €30,000: the change from $x$ to $x+1$ is
     $\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2x+1)$. With $x=2$:
     $2.1794-0.1046\times5=1.66$ percentage points
   - Fitted change from €60,000 to €70,000: with $x=6$:
     $2.1794-0.1046\times13=0.820$ percentage points. With the coefficients
     rounded to three decimals the results are 1.65 and 0.81. Both are
     correct.
   - What the two results show together: the same extra €10,000 goes with
     about half as much extra growth at the higher level of spending. The
     fitted curve becomes flatter.
3. Filled-in structure:
   - First reason: €150,000 is far outside the range of the data, whose
     largest spending is €79,900, so no venture supports the curve there.
   - Second reason: a quadratic curve keeps curving, and this one turns
     downward at about €104,000 of spending, where no data show such a
     turn.

   The turning point follows from the fitted change of part 2. The change
   from $x$ to $x+1$, $2.179-0.105(2x+1)$, is zero at $x\approx9.9$. So
   the curve is highest between €99,000 and €109,000 of spending, at about
   €104,000.
:::

```{r}
#| label: imock-q5-check
#| include: false
# Checks the answers to parts 1 to 3 of Question 5.
summary(interaction_model)$coefficients
b5 <- coef(interaction_model)
c(slope_physical = unname(b5["spend_c"]),
  slope_digital = unname(b5["spend_c"] + b5["spend_c:digitalYes"]))
bq <- coef(curve_model)
c(from_2_to_3 = unname(bq["marketing_10k"] +
                         bq["I(marketing_10k^2)"] * (2 * 2 + 1)),
  from_6_to_7 = unname(bq["marketing_10k"] +
                         bq["I(marketing_10k^2)"] * (2 * 6 + 1)))
unname(-bq["marketing_10k"] / (2 * bq["I(marketing_10k^2)"]))
max(ventures$marketing_10k)
```

## Question 6: An answer of an AI assistant (11 points)

Sara runs a young venture with a mainly digital offering. She gave column
(3) of the table in Question 4 to an AI assistant. Here is column (3) again:

```text
Outcome: sales growth (%), 320 ventures     Estimate  Std. Error
Marketing spending (€10,000s)                  1.341       0.100
Digital offering (1 = yes)                     3.084       0.463
Founder experience (years)                     0.258       0.041
Team size (members)                            0.168       0.103
Intercept                                      2.449       0.771
```

She asked: "What does this mean for my marketing budget?" The AI answered:

> "Good news. Your model controls for experience, team size, and offering
> type. So the marketing coefficient is a causal effect: if you spend
> €20,000 more on marketing, your sales growth will rise by 2.68 percentage
> points. Your venture is digital, and digital ventures grow 3.084% faster
> than the average venture."

1. Explain in one or two sentences whether the control variables in the
   model justify the claim that the marketing coefficient is a causal
   effect. Then write one sentence about €20,000 more marketing spending
   that the table does support. Use (copy and paste) this structure:
   **(6 points)**

   ```text
   Do the control variables justify the causal claim? Why:
   A sentence about €20,000 more marketing spending that the table supports:
   ```

2. The sentence about digital ventures contains two errors. Name each
   error and explain it in one sentence. Then write one correct sentence
   about the coefficient 3.084. Use (copy and paste) this structure:
   **(5 points)**

   ```text
   First error:
   Second error:
   Correct sentence about the coefficient 3.084:
   ```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Model answer

**Answers**

1. Filled-in structure:
   - Do the control variables justify the causal claim? Why: no. A control
     variable holds fixed only what is measured and in the model. Variables
     that are not in the data can influence both marketing spending and
     growth, for example the quality of the product.
   - A sentence about €20,000 more marketing spending that the table
     supports: "Among the 320 ventures, those that spend €20,000 more on
     marketing are associated with sales growth that is on average 2.68
     percentage points higher, at the same experience, team size, and
     offering type."
2. Filled-in structure:
   - First error: the outcome is in percent, so the difference is 3.084
     percentage points, not 3.084%. "3.084% faster" would be a relative
     change.
   - Second error: the comparison is with the reference category, ventures
     with a mainly physical offering, and not with the average venture.
   - Correct sentence about the coefficient 3.084: "Among the 320 ventures,
     a mainly digital offering is associated with sales growth that is on
     average 3.084 percentage points higher than a mainly physical
     offering, at the same marketing spending, experience, and team size."
:::

```{r}
#| label: imock-q6-check
#| include: false
# Checks the number of Question 6.
2 * unname(coef(col_3)["marketing_10k"])
```

you open the answers. Use the model answers to check your numbers, and
also your units, reference categories, statements about what is held fixed, and
the limits of causal claims.

## Optional: how the practice data were made (not part of the exam)

You do not need this box for any question. The practice data were made with
the code below. The fixed seed makes sure that the code always gives the
same 320 rows as the file that you download. Answer every question for the
registry data as the text describes them, not for this code.

```{r}
#| label: imock-data
set.seed(734)
n_mock <- 320
marketing_10k <- round(runif(n_mock, 0.25, 8), 2)
experience_years <- sample(0:18, n_mock, replace = TRUE)
team_size <- sample(
  1:10, n_mock, replace = TRUE,
  prob = c(8, 16, 20, 20, 14, 9, 6, 4, 2, 1)
)
digital <- factor(
  ifelse(runif(n_mock) < 0.45, "Yes", "No"),
  levels = c("No", "Yes")
)
spend_c <- marketing_10k - 4
growth_mean <-
  8 + 1.10 * spend_c + 3 * (digital == "Yes") -
  0.10 * spend_c^2 + 0.30 * experience_years +
  0.70 * spend_c * (digital == "Yes") + 0.20 * team_size
growth_pct <- round(
  growth_mean + rnorm(n_mock, 0, 2.5 + 0.40 * marketing_10k),
  2
)
ventures <- data.frame(
  growth_pct, marketing_10k, experience_years, team_size, digital, spend_c
)
```
